stem:
A 2-year-old has a thin adhesion joining the medial edges of the labia minora. She passes urine comfortably, has no postvoid dribbling and has never had a urinary infection. There is no inflammation or pain.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Surgical division under a general anaesthetic
options.explanation: An asymptomatic adhesion does not require an operation.

options.label: B
options.text: Topical oestrogen treatment with planned review
options.explanation: Oestrogen is not routine for asymptomatic fusion with easy voiding.

options.label: C
options.text: Oral antibiotics for a presumed infection
options.explanation: There are no features supporting bacterial infection.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassurance and observation without active treatment
options.explanation: Comfortable voiding and absent symptoms favour spontaneous resolution.

options.label: E
options.text: Manual separation of the adherent edges
options.explanation: Separation is painful and recurrence is common.

options.label: F
options.text: Urgent catheterisation to prevent urinary retention
options.explanation: She empties her bladder comfortably without obstruction.

options.label: G
options.text: Topical antifungal treatment for suspected candidiasis
options.explanation: The finding is adhesion, without a candidal presentation.

context:
Labial adhesions commonly reflect thin prepubertal mucosa and minor irritation. Most resolve with growth, so comfortable voiding supports observation.

If urinary outflow becomes obstructed, discuss treatment with gynaecology. Forced separation can be painful and adhesions may recur.
